title: Deuxième partie : variations sur l'équation des lacets [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois…, pages 293 à 650, dont table des matières] : notes et copies de notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from the preceding pages, §15). A finite group G acts effectively and orientation-preservingly on a surface X. Y = X/G is the quotient orbifold, with ramification indices d (written Y,d). X^! is the set of points with nontrivial stabilizer and Y^! is its image, the set of branch points. pi_1(X,G) is the equivariant fundamental group, i.e. the orbifold fundamental group. It sits in the extension 1 -> pi_1(X) -> pi_1(X,G) -> G -> 1, and (1) identifies it with pi_1(Y,d), the orbifold fundamental group of Y with cone points of orders d_b.

The previous page's Proposition sets up a bijection. On one side are the points b of Y^!. On the other are the 'maximal' outer homomorphisms phi_b : Gamma -> pi_1(X,G) lifting the inclusion of a subgroup 1 != Gamma ⊂ G. The finite subgroups Gamma involved are cyclic, namely the stabilizers G_a of the points a in the fibre X_b.

This page adds a compatibility statement, (7). Let T_b be the local loop group at b, i.e. pi_1 of a small punctured disc, abstractly Z(1). Let n = d_b. The composite T_b ⊗ Z/nZ ≅ G_a (rotation action on the tangent plane, (4)), followed by phi_a = phi_b into pi_1(X,G), followed by the iso (1) into pi_1(Y,d), is the 'truncated loop' homomorphism (2). That map sends the generator of T_b to the class of a small loop around the cone point; that class has order d_b in the orbifold group. Grothendieck's aside '(on s'en serait douté !)' marks this as expected: the local monodromy at a cone point generates the corresponding maximal finite cyclic subgroup.

Then the punctured case (8). Write X = X̂ \ S with X̂ compact and S finite, so Y = Ŷ \ T with Ŷ = X̂/G. For a cusp a in S there is the cuspidal inertia outer homomorphism k_a : T_a -> pi_1(X) -> pi_1(X,G), (9). It is to be compared with k_b : T_b -> pi_1(Y) -> pi_1(Y,d) for b = f̂(a), (10), via the canonical identification T_a ≅ T_b, (11). The next page records the resulting commutative square: it involves multiplication by the ramification index d_a.

The next page applies all this to X = U_{0,3} = P^1 minus {0,1,∞} with G = S_3. The quotient map is f = (27/4) z^2(z-1)^2/(z^2-z+1)^3, which equals 1728/j(lambda). This gives pi_1(U_{0,3}, S_3) ≅ the orbifold group of P^1 with points of orders 2, 3, ∞, i.e. the triangle/cartographic group ≅ PSL(2,Z), presented by l'_∞ l'_1 l'_0 = 1, l'_1^2 = l'_∞^3 = 1. The local generators are then matched with the order-2 and order-3 elements and with the cusp generator. The aim is to identify the S_3-equivariant fundamental group of U_{0,3} with the oriented triangulated cartographic group C^+'_{1,1} and SL(2,Z)', within the Longue Marche programme on the Teichmüller tower and Gal(Q̄/Q) actions.
errors: No mathematical error is visible on this page.

Wording inconsistency: (11) is called a canonical 'isomorphism' T_a ≅ T_b. The map actually induced by f̂ on loop groups is multiplication by d_a, which is why the next page's diagram carries a d_a·id factor. The 'isomorphism' only makes sense via the abstract identification of both groups with Z(1).
The previous page's caveat X != S^2 is needed for the splitting/fixed-point correspondence. It is implicitly assumed here and not restated.
Minor grammar: 'Supposons maintenant que X sont de la forme'.

ideas.what: In the orbifold fundamental group, the maximal finite cyclic subgroups (up to conjugacy) correspond to cone points, and each is generated by the local loop truncated mod d_b.
ideas.modern_name: Elliptic elements of Fuchsian/orbifold groups; local inertia at cone points
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical Fuchsian group theory (Poincaré, Fricke–Klein); orbifold formalism by Thurston (1970s)
ideas.where_published: Closely related remarks in La Longue Marche (1981) and Esquisse d'un programme (1984) on cartographic groups; exact statement unsure

ideas.what: Conjugacy classes of finite-order splittings of 1 -> pi_1(X) -> pi_1(X,G) -> G correspond to fixed points (a topological 'section conjecture' for finite group actions).
ideas.modern_name: Fixed points ↔ conjugacy classes of sections for finite group actions; cf. 'cuspidal/finite sections' in anabelian geometry
ideas.usually_credited_to: Topologically classical (Nielsen, Kerckhoff era); étale analogues discussed by Nakamura, Mochizuki, Hoshi and others
ideas.where_published: Grothendieck's 1983 letter to Faltings mentions fixed points/sections in the anabelian context; precise statement unsure

ideas.what: Compatibility of cuspidal inertia under a ramified G-quotient: the inertia at a maps to the d_a-th power of the inertia at b.
ideas.modern_name: Behaviour of inertia/decomposition under tame ramified covers
ideas.where_published: SGA1 (étale analogue); SGA1 Exp. XIII (tame fundamental group, Grothendieck–Murre)

ideas.what: The S_3-quotient of P^1 minus 3 points via f = 1728/j, identifying pi_1(U_{0,3}, S_3) with the (2,3,∞) triangle group ≅ PSL(2,Z) / cartographic group C^+_{1,1}.
ideas.modern_name: Lambda-to-j covering; Γ(2) ⊂ PSL(2,Z) with quotient S_3; cartographic groups
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Klein, Dedekind); cartographic-group viewpoint Grothendieck, Esquisse d'un programme
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme §§2–3 (cartographic groups, SL(2,Z) and Belyi/dessins)

deep.surprise_reason: Careful but routine bookkeeping: inertia at cone points and cusps in orbifold fundamental groups, set up in order to identify the S_3-equivariant pi_1 of P^1 minus 3 points with PSL(2,Z)/cartographic groups. All of this is classical or already in Grothendieck's circulated programme.

'Considérons alors, pour tout a ∈ S, l'hom extérieur' — confirmed (the a is written over a b).
In (8), after 'Y = Ŷ \ T' there is a crossed-out symbol before 'avec'; then 'Ŷ = X̂/G'.
